title: 2025-11-04-masking-and-retention-toggle-deep-dive-evercrest-energy
meeting_header: Date: 2025-11-04 | Start: 15:00 UTC | Duration: 58m | Attendees: Sofia Alvarez (Redwood AE), Brian Cho (Redwood SE), Maya Patel (Evercrest), Liam O'Reilly (Evercrest), Grace Zhao (Evercrest)
summary: Demo focused on per-request storage toggles, policy-based masking, and retention controls in the Redwood Console and API. Walked through console toggles, API flags for ephemeral request storage, example masking rules, KMS integration and options for private deployments; discussed tradeoffs for batching/caching vs retention for cost/latency. Agreed next steps: share security whitepaper, pilot plan, and pricing for dedicated capacity.
topics: Console: data handling toggles and audit logs
Masking rules and regex-based PII redaction
Optimize: batching vs short retention tradeoffs
action_items: Sofia Alvarez - Send security whitepaper + SOC2/ISO artifacts - 2025-11-06
Brian Cho - Export of example masking rules and sample cURL for ephemeral storage flag - 2025-11-05
Maya Patel - Share sample prompt/PII patterns for pilot - 2025-11-07
next_steps: Provide dedicated pricing ballpark for 3-node reserved pool and private deployment checklist
Run small benchmark of 100k tokens with and without prefix caching to show cost delta
transcript:
[00:00] Sofia Alvarez: Hey everyone, thanks for joining. It's Sofia and Brian from Redwood. How's everyone doing?
[00:05] Maya Patel: Good, thanks. Busy Q4 but excited to see how you handle our retention concerns.
[00:10] Brian Cho: Awesome. Quick agenda — we're going to walk through the Console toggles for request storage, then show API flags you can set per-request, and finally a short Optimize demo that highlights cost/latency tradeoffs when you enable caching.
[00:20] Liam O'Reilly: Real quick — our primary ask is that for any PII-containing prompts, we do not persist raw requests in logs by default, and we need audit trails for any stored items.
[00:30] Grace Zhao: And from Security side, SOC2 evidence, KMS integration, SSO with SAML, and RBAC are must-haves.
[00:40] Sofia Alvarez: Totally. Brian, can you share your screen and pull up the Console?
[00:47] Brian Cho: Yep — sharing. Okay, this is the Redwood Console > Data Controls. You can see toggles at the top — default retention, request_storage: on/off, and a per-route override. Notice the little info icon that explains ephemeral versus persisted storage.
[01:10] Maya Patel: That per-route override is interesting. Can a route be tied to a service account or to an API key?
[01:17] Brian Cho: Good question. Routes tie to an API key. You can create keys with baked-in policies — like never-store, mask-first, or redact-then-store. So at runtime you can choose a key which enforces a policy.
[01:32] Liam O'Reilly: Is that enforced server-side or client-side? We need to know it can't be bypassed.
[01:36] Brian Cho: Server-side enforcement. Keys are bound to policies in the control plane. Even if you call the hosted API directly, the server will apply the policy before any write to long-term storage.
[01:46] Grace Zhao: What about streaming? We use streaming to reduce latency; does streaming payloads get captured in logs?
[01:52] Sofia Alvarez: By default the streaming events are ephemeral — they flow through the runtime and the default retention is zero for streaming unless you explicitly opt-in for a session snapshot. There's a separate toggle for session-level snapshots.
[02:05] Brian Cho: I'll flip into the API example — here's a sample cURL: curl https://api.redwood.ai/v1/generate -H 'Authorization: Bearer KEY' -d '{"input":"...","request_storage":"ephemeral","masking_policy":"pii-first"}' 
[02:25] Maya Patel: Wait, 'masking_policy' — is that a pre-defined rule or can we upload custom regexes?
[02:30] Brian Cho: Both. We provide a collection of curated policies — email, SSN, credit card, phone — and you can add custom rules using regex or a small policy DSL. Important note: masking runs synchronously in the inference path when you pick mask-first policy, which adds a small latency (typically 10–30ms for standard payloads).
[02:50] Liam O'Reilly: That latency is fine if it's deterministic. Can we see a quick demo of a rule that redacts account numbers?
[02:55] Brian Cho: Sure — I'll switch to the Masking rules page. Here is a sample rule: pattern: (\b\d{4}-\d{4}-\d{4}-\d{4}\b) -> mask with Xs. I'm going to run an example via the API console.
[03:15] [03:15] Brian Cho (typing): Posting a request... response back in 220ms. Request body contained a credit card pattern; we replaced middle digits with **** and persisted a redacted copy to the audit log.
[03:28] Maya Patel: When you say 'persisted a redacted copy', what fields are stored in the audit log? Full metadata? Is original raw text stored in any tmp storage?
[03:36] Brian Cho: Audit logs store the redacted input, model used, tokens consumed, timestamp, and request id. Original raw text is never written to long-term storage if you choose mask-first or never-store. It may transit memory during processing but is not written to disk.
[03:48] Grace Zhao: Transit memory — is that encrypted at rest? And do you have HSM-backed keys?
[03:52] Brian Cho: Data in memory is not at-rest encrypted but is protected by process isolation. For persisted artifacts we integrate with KMS — you can bring your own key (BYOK) and have it backed by HSM through supported cloud KMS providers. For Redwood Private, you can use your internal HSM.
[04:10] Liam O'Reilly: How about auditability — can we export logs to our SIEM?
[04:14] Brian Cho: Yes, we support streaming audit events to your Kafka or S3 (with encryption) and there are connectors for Splunk/Datadog. You can also enable immutable audit snapshots for compliance reviews.
[04:25] Maya Patel: Cool. Can the Console show retention lifetime per key? I'd like to set a 7-day retention that auto-purges.
[04:32] Brian Cho: Absolutely, you can set retention in days per key or per-route. We also have a 'purge window' where deletes are scheduled and then securely wiped (depending on deployment). In Private you control the purge mechanism fully.
[04:46] [04:46] Sofia Alvarez: Quick interjection: many customers ask about the tradeoff between caching (which saves cost and latency) and our zero-retention posture. Brian, can you demo how Optimize suggests a config change?
[04:56] Brian Cho: Yup — opening Redwood Optimize. Here you can upload a sample workload or use the live stream. Optimize analyzes sequence lengths and suggests enabling prefix caching for deterministic prompts — it shows an estimated token-cost reduction of ~36% for the workload you uploaded, but flags that caching requires storing prefixes in cache which meets your retention policy if you allow short-term KV cache retention.
[05:20] Liam O'Reilly: How short is short-term? Milliseconds, seconds, minutes? Our compliance team wants to limit to under 24 hours.
[05:27] Brian Cho: Cache TTL is configurable; typical production TTLs are 5–15 minutes, but you can set it to zero to disable. For customers wanting under 24 hours, that's straightforward. We log cache hits as metrics but not the content unless you opt into cache diagnostics.
[05:41] Maya Patel: If we disable storage but enable caching, is the cache considered storage?
[05:46] Brian Cho: In our policy model, cache is distinct from persisted storage. We treat cache as ephemeral in-memory K V cache. If you have 'never-store' policy it will still allow ephemeral in-memory KV caching unless you explicitly set 'disable_runtime_cache'. So you can enforce no caching via key policy if needed.
[06:02] Grace Zhao: We will probably want to run a pilot where caching is enabled for a subset of traffic to measure latency improvements, while never storing for other critical routes.
[06:09] Sofia Alvarez: Perfect — that was the plan we wanted to propose. 
[06:15] [06:15] Brian Cho (screen): Now switching to API flags for a per-request override. Example 1: request_storage: "never" and masking_policy: "mask-first". Example 2: request_storage: "ephemeral" and session_snapshot: "on-demand".
[06:33] Liam O'Reilly: If a request has request_storage:"never" and the model errors, is there any diagnostic info we can get? We need observability to triage.
[06:40] Brian Cho: If never-store is set we still write anonymized traces (no content) with trace ids and token counts. For deeper debugging you can opt-in to 'debug-store' for a specific API key or a temporary job but that data is then subject to retention and your policy. We also support redacted-stack traces — e.g., redact PII before bubbling to logs.
[06:58] Maya Patel: What about legal holds — can we prevent automatic purge for a flagged request?
[07:03] Brian Cho: Yes, there is an 'eDiscovery' flag that marks items as preserved. It's controlled by RBAC — only allowed roles can set legal-hold which prevents purge until cleared.
[07:12] Grace Zhao: On the topic of RBAC — can we sync with our IdP for Okta? We need group-based permissions for who can change retention.
[07:18] Brian Cho: We have SAML2.0/SCIM integration; you can sync groups and map them to console roles. You can make a group that only has 'read-audit' without 'retention-modify'.
[07:26] Liam O'Reilly: Great. From infra side, if we go Redwood Private in our VPC, where does the control plane live?
[07:32] Brian Cho: For Private deployments, the control plane can be customer-managed in their VPC; instead of sending keys to Redwood we can deploy the control plane as a managed appliance. Networking and KMS calls can be backhauled to your KMS. There's a small ops package for on-prem installs.
[07:48] Maya Patel: Do you have any references for SOC2 artifacts we can share with our auditors?
[07:52] Sofia Alvarez: Yes — I'll drop the security whitepaper and SOC2 attestation in the follow-up. There's also a short checklist for auditors.
[07:59] [08:00] Liam O'Reilly: Can we talk about pricing impacts? If we store redacted inputs instead of raw, does that change billing for token usage?
[08:08] Brian Cho: Billing is based on tokens computed at inference time; storing redacted copies doesn't change token billing. There is additional storage cost if you persist logs, obviously, but for most setups the storage cost is tiny relative to token cost. Optimize can estimate storage overhead in the cost model.
[08:25] Maya Patel: For the pilot we want 3 routes: internal dev (no storage), customer-facing chat (mask-first + short retention), and analytics (persist redacted + export to S3). Would that map to three API keys with different policies?
[08:36] Brian Cho: Exactly. You'd create three keys with their policy bindings. We'll show a sample key policy YAML in the follow-up.
[08:45] [08:45] Sofia Alvarez: Let's do a quick live test using the API playground to simulate an inbound customer chat message with an email and account number. Brian?
[08:52] [09:00] Brian Cho (typing): Sending request... (pause) Response returned. Transcript: 'Hi, my account is 1234-5678-9012, please help.' The masking policy replaced the number with [REDACTED] and the audit entry contains the redacted body.
[09:15] Maya Patel: Can you show the audit entry?
[09:19] Brian Cho: Pulling audit viewer — here's the entry: Timestamp, route, redacted_input: 'Hi, my account is [REDACTED] ...', model: 'redwood-llama-3-70b', tokens: 78.
[09:34] Liam O'Reilly: Do you keep a mapping anywhere that would allow us to restore the redacted value later if needed?
[09:39] Brian Cho: No, masking is one-way by default. If you want reversible tokenization you'd need to enable token vaulting which is a separate product feature that stores encrypted tokens with BYOK. That's more for customer-managed forensic use-cases.
[09:56] Grace Zhao: We might need reversible lookups for support use-cases but only with strict RBAC and audit trails. Is token vaulting on roadmap?
[10:02] Brian Cho: It is — we can include it as an enterprise option in the pilot scope.
[10:08] Maya Patel: Switching topics — GDPR/data residency. We are EU customers, some data must stay in EU. Do you support region-specific retention?
[10:16] Sofia Alvarez: Yes, region policies exist. You can pin routes to specific regions, and for Hosted we have EU regions; for Private you control the physical location entirely.
[10:25] Liam O'Reilly: We need proofs because auditors will ask where the data physically resides.
[10:29] Sofia Alvarez: We'll provide the region map and a compliance packet that lists where logs and backups are stored per region.
[10:36] [10:36] Brian Cho: Back to Optimize briefly — you can run a simulation that toggles cache on/off and see the latency and cost delta. I ran a quick sim earlier for Evercrest-like traffic and the console shows average latency drop from 220ms to 160ms when enabling prefix caching for 42% of requests. Cost estimate shows about 28% token-cost reduction, but you do trade some short-term cache footprint.
[10:57] Maya Patel: That's compelling. We'll want to measure with our actual traffic.
[11:02] Sofia Alvarez: Agreed. We'll propose a pilot where we split traffic A/B and run for two weeks.
[11:07] [11:07] Grace Zhao: A couple of small technical clarifications — 1) If we integrate BYOK with Google KMS, are encryption keys rotated automatically? 2) Do you support hardware-backed keys only or software keys too?
[11:18] Brian Cho: You can bring either. Cloud KMS providers offer hardware-backed keys; if you want HSM-backed exclusively you can leverage our Private deployment. Keys rotated per your KMS policy; Redwood will call Encrypt/Decrypt with your KMS at runtime, we don't persist the plaintext key.
[11:33] Liam O'Reilly: Any limits on request rate for key operations? We worry about KMS call quotas adding latency.
[11:38] Brian Cho: We recommend caching encrypted material and minimizing KMS calls — for example, we cache the data encryption keys (DEKs) for a short TTL and rotate them per policy. That avoids per-request KMS calls.
[11:50] Maya Patel: Could you touch on egress — if logs are exported to S3, are they encrypted server-side or client-side?
[11:57] Brian Cho: Both supported. You can have server-side encryption with SSE-KMS or provide client-side encrypted payloads. For compliance, most customers choose SSE-KMS with their own key.
[12:08] [12:08] Sofia Alvarez: I'd like to surface a common objection — some teams worry that masking-first can still leak structured PII in model outputs if prompts are not sanitized. Brian, any recommendations?
[12:20] Brian Cho: Yes — combine mask-first on input with output filters and model steering. Redwood's post-generation hygiene layer runs a second pass to redact any detected PII in responses before returning to the user. You can add a red-team prompt set to the Optimize eval suite to monitor regressions.
[12:40] Grace Zhao: Do you provide alerts when a post-generation filter triggers?
[12:44] Brian Cho: Yep — console has alerting for hygiene triggers with counts and sample redacted text (not the raw). You can hook alerts into Slack or PagerDuty.
[12:53] Liam O'Reilly: For the pilot, we'll want the alerting wired into our monitoring and a daily digest for the Security team.
[12:59] Sofia Alvarez: We'll include that in the implementation plan.
[13:03] [13:03] Maya Patel: One more question before we wrap the demo: How does Redwood handle backups? If we have persisted redacted logs, do backups also contain redacted copies and do you have retention controls for backups?
[13:14] Brian Cho: Backups inherit retention policies and are stored encrypted; this is all documented in the backup policy. You can disable backups for certain retention classes in Private.
[13:25] Grace Zhao: Okay thanks. This is helpful.
[13:28] Sofia Alvarez: Let's move to a short Q&A and then summarize next steps.
[13:33] [13:33] Maya Patel: On the practical side — we have a procurement timeline: if the pilot goes well, procurement wants to close a Dedicated pool purchase by end of Q1. Any blockers on your side?
[13:42] Sofia Alvarez: No blockers — we'll need a procurement POC and legal contact for the SOW and the Data Processing Agreement. We'll send templates.
[13:49] Liam O'Reilly: Legal will ask about sub-processors. Are you using any third-party log processors?
[13:55] Brian Cho: We use third-party telemetry providers for metrics; audit logs you can choose to export to your S3 to avoid third-party storage. We'll list sub-processors in the compliance packet.
[14:06] Maya Patel: All right — high level recap and action items?
[14:10] Sofia Alvarez: Recap: 1) Console has per-key/per-route retention and request_storage flags. 2) Mask-first policy redacts before persistence. 3) Cache is configurable and can be disabled to meet zero-cache policies. 4) BYOK/KMS and region pinning supported. 5) Optimize can simulate cost/latency tradeoffs.
[14:29] Sofia Alvarez: Action items were: we'll send security docs, sample masking rules, pricing ballpark, and the pilot plan. Maya, you'll share expected prompt patterns for the pilot.
[14:40] Maya Patel: Yes. Expect an email by Friday with sample data.
[14:44] [14:44] Brian Cho: I'll add the sample cURLs and key policy YAML to the follow-up.
[14:49] Grace Zhao: We'll review and get back with any follow-ups.
[14:53] Sofia Alvarez: Great. Thanks everyone. We'll schedule the pilot kickoff for next week — expecting about a 30-minute setup call.
[14:59] Maya Patel: Thanks, bye.
[15:00] Liam O'Reilly: Thanks all. Bye.
notes: Transcription has occasional mis-hear — e.g., 'K V cache' instead of KV cache; speaker timestamps approximate. Conversation included compliance, developer ergonomics, and a concrete pilot plan.
